Python API reference

Everything below is importable directly from the top-level package:

from hypertiler import TileMaker, inkTile, write_svg, write_png, regular_vectors, classify_areas, make_colors

See Quickstart: using HyperTiler as a library for worked examples using each of these together.

Building tilings

hypertiler.regular_vectors(fold, shift='regular')[source]

Build a vector_data array for a regular fold-fold grid.

Each row is (tile_length, grid_length, angle_degrees, shift) - the format TileMaker expects, with angles evenly spaced around the circle. shift matches the GUI’s “Grid shifts” options:

  • ‘regular’: alternating +/-1/(fold/2) for even fold, or 1/fold for odd fold - the default, and what most named regular tilings use.

  • ‘zero’: no shift at all - the degenerate/singular case.

  • ‘random’: shifts drawn uniformly from (-1, 1), independent per vector.

  • ‘regular_random’: random shifts that sum to 1 across the whole set.

class hypertiler.TileMaker(vector_data, grid_len)[source]
classmethod build_grid(vector_data, grid_len)[source]

Just the grid-line construction (dedupe + sort + Grids), with no tile/intersection computation at all.

Substitution (inflation) tilings

apply_transform_to_points(points, transform_type, nums)[source]
parse_svg(filename)[source]

Parse an inflation-rules SVG file.

Layers labelled ‘super<type>’ define supertile templates; layers labelled ‘sub<type>’ define subtile placements.

Returns:

  • tiling (dict - raw group data)

  • types (dict - stroke-color -> tile-type)

parse_seed_svg(filename, types, supertiles)[source]

Parse a seed SVG containing pre-placed tiles.

Tiles are identified by fill color (using the types mapping from the rules SVG). The seed may be drawn at any consistent scale (supertile size, subtile size, or otherwise) – the actual scale factor is inferred by comparing the first seed tile’s own edge length to its type’s already-normalized (unity-edge) template in supertiles, the same trick globalScale itself is derived with. Group transforms are applied recursively.

Returns a list of (tile_type, coords) tuples.

rename_tiles_by_type(tiling, names)[source]

Rename tile keys to standardised type_N form using fill-color mapping.

find_min_edge_length(tiles)[source]
normalize_tiles(tiles, scale)[source]
extract_rules(supertile, subtiles)[source]

Build substitution rules: each entry is [sub_scale, sub_center, angle].

apply_rule(tile_type, coords, rules, supertiles)[source]

Inflate one tile into its subtiles. Returns list of (new_type, new_coords) tuples.

remove_duplicates(tiles, tol=0.01)[source]

Remove duplicate tiles based on centre position.

substitute(initial_tiles, rules, supertiles, generations=1)[source]

Apply recursive substitution; returns [(tile_type, coords), …].

Helpers

hypertiler.classify_areas(areas)[source]

Bucket raw tile areas into integer type indices.

Tiles of the same underlying shape/type share (near-)identical area in these tilings, so rounding to 3 decimal places and taking the unique values gives a stable type label per tile - this is the same logic the GUI uses to decide how many colours a tiling needs.

Returns (type_idx, unique_areas): type_idx is an int array parallel to areas, and unique_areas are the distinct rounded area values.

hypertiler.make_colors(n, scheme='default', base_color='#4a6fa5')[source]

Generate n visually distinct RGB colours for colouring tile types.

This is the same colour generation the GUI uses to pick tile colours when you don’t hand-pick your own - handy for a quick palette without designing one yourself.

Parameters:

  • n (int) – Number of colours to generate.

  • scheme ({'default', 'tonal'}) – ‘default’ steps hue around the full colour wheel (golden-ratio spacing from a random starting hue) - what the GUI uses unless you switch its colour scheme preference. ‘tonal’ instead generates n tones/shades of a single base colour.

  • base_color (str) – Hex colour (e.g. ‘#4a6fa5’), only used when scheme=’tonal’.

Return type:

list of (r, g, b) tuples, each channel in 0-255.

hypertiler.write_svg(filepath, polys, colors, edge_color=(0, 0, 0), edge_width=1.0)[source]

Write polygons as fill-coloured SVG paths.

Parameters:

  • polys (list of (N, 2) coordinate arrays, one polygon per tile.)

  • colors (list of (r, g, b) 0-255 tuples, one per polygon in polys.)

  • edge_color (stroke applied to every tile; edge_width <= 0) – omits the stroke entirely.

  • edge_width (stroke applied to every tile; edge_width <= 0) – omits the stroke entirely.

hypertiler.write_png(filepath, polys, colors, edge_color=(0, 0, 0), edge_width=1, size=(1000, 1000), background=(255, 255, 255))[source]

Rasterize polygons to a PNG image.

Unlike write_svg, edge_width here is in output pixels directly - there’s no data-unit-vs-pixel ambiguity for a raster image the way there is for an SVG’s own coordinate space.

Parameters:

  • polys (as in write_svg.)

  • colors (as in write_svg.)

  • edge_color (stroke applied to every tile, in pixels;) – edge_width <= 0 omits the stroke entirely.

  • edge_width (stroke applied to every tile, in pixels;) – edge_width <= 0 omits the stroke entirely.

  • size ((width, height) of the output image in pixels. The tiling is) – scaled to fit within this box (preserving aspect ratio, with a 5% margin) and centred.

  • background (RGB fill for the area outside the tiling.)
